## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design runtime-extensible systems using the Command pattern and a registry to enable plugins.

## Key Concepts
- Command pattern, Registry, Dynamic plugin loading, Fault isolation, Help generation

## Code Example
```javascript
// Implementation sketch
interface Command { name: string; description: string; run(args: string[]): Promise<void>; }
class CommandRegistry { private commands = new Map<string, Command>(); register(c: Command){ this.commands.set(c.name, c); } get(name: string){ return this.commands.get(name); } list(){ return [...this.commands.values()]; } }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you secure plugin loading and sandbox execution?
- How would you handle conflicting command names and versioning?

```typescript
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How to model evaluation order and short-circuit semantics?
- How to handle cross-feature conflicts and auditing of evaluator registrations?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Beginner-friendly exploration of extensibility and non-blocking I/O: add new sinks without changing core, and isolate failures per sink.

## Key Concepts
- Strategy/Plug-in pattern for runtime extension
- Registry mapping names to Sink implementations
- Non-blocking writes via per-sink queuing and worker pool
- Fault isolation and graceful degradation

## Code Example
```typescript
interface Sink { write(msg: string): Promise<void> }
class Registry { addSink(name: string, s: Sink): void; getSinks(): Sink[] }
class Logger { constructor(private reg: Registry) ; log(msg: string): void { for (const s of reg.getSinks()) s.write(msg); } }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test sink isolation and backpressure?
- How would you implement graceful shutdown for all sinks?
